title: Truth teaches (I.3)
hook: every review of a restaurant, and one bite settles it: happy is he whom truth itself teaches
tomorrow: a rumor hits the group chat. what do you do before you forward it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two Latin words in a chapter about learning: ama nesciri, love to be unknown. The line was unknown.

You can read every review of a restaurant, the photos, the arguments about the sauce, and still not know what it tastes like. One bite settles it. Some things only arrive firsthand. Chapter three of The Imitation of Christ opens on exactly that kind of learning. Happy, it says, is the one whom truth itself teaches: not through passing pictures and words, but as it really is.
screen: `EVERY REVIEW, NO TASTE.` → `ONE BITE SETTLES IT.` → `TRUTH ITSELF TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Inside the Church, two views meet on this chapter, and both have a strong case. The first is the chapter's own warning. What good is arguing over hidden, obscure things, it asks, when we won't be asked about them at the judgment? On that day we won't be asked what we read, but what we did; not how well we spoke, but how well we lived. Where are the famous masters now? Others hold their places, and hardly anyone remembers them. O how quickly, it sighs, the glory of the world passes. The second view says: careful. Without study you can fool yourself, mistake a feeling for the truth, or follow whoever speaks loudest. The Catechism says faith and reason never truly contradict each other, since the same God gives both. And here the chapter surprises its own readers. It agrees. Learning isn't to be blamed, it says, nor simple knowledge of anything; it's good, and ordered by God. But a good conscience and a good life come first. And the truth that teaches isn't a feeling. The chapter calls it the eternal Word, the one John's Gospel names, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
screen: `ASKED WHAT WE DID, NOT READ.` · `WITHOUT STUDY, YOU FOOL YOURSELF.` · `LEARNING ISN'T BLAMED; LIFE FIRST.` · `THE TRUTH IS THE WORD.` · then, large: `TRUTH ITSELF TEACHES.`

segments.voice: If there's water nearby, take one slow sip and notice what it's actually like: cool or warm, its weight, the swallow. No description of water could have handed you that. Let the rest of the sit be firsthand in the same way, taking whatever is here just as it is.
Truth teaches. Chapter three's blessing on learning that comes firsthand, from the Word himself, with a good life first.
Keep this one: truth itself teaches, and it teaches best the one who's living what they learn. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics study the faith through scripture, the Catechism and the Church's teachers, and also pray, since the Church teaches that faith and reason come from the same God and that a holy life is the goal of both.

fork.setup: two friends argue at youth group. Ana says skip the theology books; prayer and a good life are what count. Ben says without study you'll fool yourself. what's chapter three's actual position?
options: learning isn't blamed, but a good conscience and life come first.
Ana's right: books are a trap, and only experience can teach.
Ben's right: the more you know, the holier you become.
fork.reveal: the chapter warns against learning without living, and also says plain knowledge is good and ordered by God. both friends hold half of it.

The Imitation of Christ.meaning: a short book of counsel credited to Thomas à Kempis

Catechism.meaning: the Catholic Church's summary of its teaching

the eternal Word.meaning: Christ, as John's Gospel names him: the Word who was God

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English Bible translation

notes: Imitation I.3 paraphrased throughout: happy is he whom truth teaches by itself, not by figures and passing words but as it is; what good is disputing hidden and obscure things we won't be reproved for ignoring at the judgment; we shall be asked not what we read but what we did, not how well we spoke but how religiously we lived; where are the masters and doctors now?; O how quickly the glory of the world passes; learning is not to be blamed, nor the mere knowledge of anything, which is good and ordained by God, but a good conscience and virtuous life are always preferred; from the one Word are all things.
